I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

I have failed in my most important role in life
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'physical abuse by romantic partner', the appraisal 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' is clinically hard to reconcile because this trauma does not ordinarily involve other deaths or a mass-casualty context. The rest of the profile centers on partner violence, hypervigilance, and fragmented visual recall, so this item introduces a markedly different trauma scenario without support elsewhere in the selected items.

'Car sounds' is difficult to connect clinically to the rest of this profile for physical abuse by a romantic partner. The other trigger items and all threat, memory, and appraisal items center on interpersonal trauma, bodily alarm, betrayal, and fragmented terror-based recall. A car-sound trigger suggests a different trauma context unless there is supporting material elsewhere, so this item is the main coherence concern.

vignette: Arun Singh, a 41‑year‑old architect from San Diego, began the night of his first visit to the clinic with the memory of a sudden, violent blow from the woman he loved. The day had been ordinary—he had returned from a client site, still humming the sketch of a new residential concept, and was about to join his wife, Priya, for dinner. The argument had erupted over a misinterpreted comment about his design choice. In a fit of rage, she struck him on the jaw, the sound of her clenched teeth echoing in his ears. As the impact landed, Arun felt a sharp, jarring ache, a wave of nausea, and the room suddenly smelled of old wine and burnt alcohol, the scent of Priya’s earlier evening drinks lingering on her clothes. That smell, the incoherent chatter of her friends in the hallway, and the sudden, throbbing discomfort in his stomach all acted as triggers, immediately launching his body into a state of heightened threat: his heart hammered, his shoulders tensed, and his eyes darted for an escape route. He could not pause to think; the body's reaction came before any rational assessment, leaving him stunned and trembling even before the memory of the slap fully surfaced. The experience of feeling physically unwell, the disorienting voices around him, and the sharp scent of alcohol had all provoked the same instant surge of danger he felt that night, illustrating how everyday sensory cues could trigger his acute sense of threat. For weeks after, Arun found himself haunted by those triggers. Each time he walked past a bar or caught a whiff of alcohol at a friend's gathering, his stomach turned, his hands shook, and the image of Priya’s fist rose up before his eyes. The memory of that terrifying moment replayed in his mind with photographic clarity, each flash as vivid as a picture. The terror of that night was not a distant past; when he smelled alcohol, the terror would return, forcing him to relive the exact sensations he had felt in the moment—his heart pounding, his body on edge, the sharp sting of the blow. The intensity of the threat he experienced during recall intensified his sense of danger in the present, and the memory itself reinforced his belief that he had failed as a husband and partner, that he could not protect himself or keep the harmony in his most important role. These self‑doubts spiraled, making him more vigilant and alert, further raising the threat level whenever he sensed danger. The more threatened he felt, the more the memories resurfaced with brutal detail, feeding back into his self‑doubt. At the same time, every instance where he sensed a threat—whether a sudden noise or a vague feeling of unease—would trigger a physical response that left him feeling ill, setting off a new cycle of triggers, threat, and negative appraisal. In this way, the triggers led to threat, the threat to memory, the memory to negative appraisal, and the negative appraisal back to threat, creating a self‑reinforcing loop that had begun to dominate his daily life. As the months stretched on, Arun’s professional environment became a battleground. He would often be on construction sites or in office meetings when a distant clatter of machinery or a whispered conversation about client budgets would set his body in motion: his heart accelerated, his mind raced to assess danger, and his shoulders clamped tight. The threat he felt made him feel physically ill even before he could fully register the event, and the feeling of sickness would, in turn, heighten his sense of threat. Each instance of perceived danger would trigger the memory of Priya’s attack, the same terror and the same catastrophic self‑appraisals that he had come to fear. He avoided social gatherings where the scent of alcohol was common, and he began missing important project deadlines because he could not bring himself to sit in meetings where voices were raised. The loss of these professional opportunities fed into his sense of failure as an architect, further entrenching his negative self‑beliefs. The pattern continued: triggers produced threat, threat amplified memory, memory fueled negative appraisals, and negative appraisals heightened threat, which in turn produced more triggers—a tightly interwoven cycle that left Arun feeling trapped, his body and mind constantly on high alert. Finally, the compounding effects of sleep loss and chronic anxiety took a toll. He found it increasingly difficult to fall asleep because he could not allow his mind to let go; he would wake up with his heart racing and his senses sharp, convinced that danger lurked in the dark. The fear of being betrayed by the one person he had trusted, coupled with a relentless self‑doubt about his capacity to fulfill his most important role, made him realize that his life had been hijacked by a past injury. The day he finally reached out for help, he was terrified that he might relive the pain in therapy and that the therapist might not understand the cultural nuances of his experience. Yet he also hoped for relief, for a chance to reclaim his health, his career, and the sense of control he had lost.
